subject: community-medicine
title: Concept of Health: WHO Definition, Positive Health and Determinants

steps.title: The WHO definition word by word
steps.tx: The **WHO definition of health** from 1948 describes health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. Later wording added the ability to lead a socially and economically productive life. Exams test the three named dimensions and the year, so quote the sentence exactly and note what it leaves out.
steps.say: Start with the sentence itself. Health means complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just having no disease. That wording dates from 1948, and a later addition speaks of leading a socially and economically productive life.

rows: Body structure and function at their best
Mind at ease, able to cope and decide
Full part in family and community life
Health is more than a negative state

steps.title: Why critics call the definition too broad
steps.tx: Critics argue that **complete well-being** sets a bar almost nobody reaches on a given day, so most people would count as unhealthy. They also object that health is framed as a fixed state, while real health shifts with age, illness and recovery. The definition still guides policy because it points beyond clinics toward living conditions, work and social support.
steps.say: Now hear the other side. If health needs complete well-being, almost everyone falls short every day. Health also moves up and down over a lifetime, yet the sentence sounds fixed. It survives because it pushes policy toward housing, work and social life, not clinics alone.

left.title: Strengths of the WHO wording
points: Positive goal, not just no disease
Covers mind and society, not body alone

steps.title: Positive health as the top of the scale
steps.tx: **Positive health** means every cell and organ working at optimum capacity in harmony, with a mind that feels mastery over its surroundings and a social life with full participation. Teachers call it a mirage because adaptation never ends: infection, ageing and stress keep shifting the target. The idea still matters, since services aim higher than survival after illness.
steps.say: Picture the top end of the scale. Body systems work at their best together, the person feels in control, and social participation is complete. Teachers call that a mirage because life keeps changing the target, yet the idea lifts care above mere survival.

rows: Every organ at optimum capacity in harmony
Sense of well-being and mastery over surroundings
Full capacity to participate in the social system

steps.title: The spectrum from positive health to death
steps.tx: The **spectrum of health** places positive health at the top, then better health, freedom from sickness, unrecognised sickness, mild sickness, severe sickness and death at the bottom. Movement runs both ways: treatment, rest and rehabilitation pull a person upward, while new exposures push downward. No sharp line separates health from sickness, which is why borderline findings need clinical judgement.
steps.say: Lay the levels out in order. Positive health sits at the top and death at the bottom, with freedom from sickness and grades of sickness between. People move up with treatment and rest, and down after new harm. No single line divides the healthy from the sick.

steps.tx: **Spectrum of health** runs as a single horizontal bar from positive health, through better health and freedom from sickness, into unrecognised, mild and severe sickness, ending at death. Arrows point both ways. Treatment, rest and rehabilitation move a person toward the healthy pole, whereas a new exposure drives the opposite way. Health and sickness share no sharp boundary, so a borderline finding still needs judgement.

steps.title: Four changing concepts of health
steps.tx: Four concepts frame exam answers on the **biomedical concept**, which equates health with absence of disease under germ theory. The ecological concept sees a dynamic equilibrium between people and surroundings. The psychosocial concept adds social, cultural and economic forces. The holistic concept joins all three and echoes a sound mind in a sound body within a sound family and environment.
steps.say: Four labels organise this history. Biomedical thinking equates health with no disease. Ecological thinking stresses balance with surroundings. Psychosocial thinking adds culture and economics. Holistic thinking joins them all, echoing a sound mind in a sound body, family and environment.

rows: Hard to apply at the bedside

steps.title: Dimensions examiners ask by name
steps.tx: The **physical dimension** shows in good complexion, clean skin, bright eyes, sound sleep, good appetite and regular bowel and bladder action, with pulse, blood pressure and exercise tolerance in the normal range. Mental health means balance within oneself and with others. Social health means fulfilling relationships and a useful role. Spiritual, emotional and vocational dimensions complete the usual list.
steps.say: Examiners love named dimensions. Physical signs include clear skin, bright eyes, sound sleep and normal pulse and blood pressure. Mental health means inner balance. Social health means real relationships and a role. Spiritual, emotional and vocational dimensions round out the list.

rows: Normal pulse, blood pressure and exercise tolerance
Balance within self and with others
Fulfilling relationships and a useful role

steps.title: Determinants inside the person
steps.tx: **Biological determinants** begin with the genes a person inherits, which set susceptibility to conditions such as colour blindness, diabetes and chromosomal disorders. Ageing itself changes risk, as tissues wear and immunity falls. Sex also patterns disease: some disorders cluster in men, others in women. None of these can be rewritten, so prevention works around them with screening and early care.
steps.say: Some determinants travel with the person. Genes set susceptibility to diabetes, colour blindness and chromosomal disorders. Ageing raises risk as immunity falls, and sex patterns many diseases. Since none of these change, prevention answers with screening and early care.

steps.tx: **Biological determinants** sit at the centre of the wheel: inherited genes (colour blindness, diabetes, chromosomal disorders), ageing that wears tissues and lowers immunity, and sex, which clusters some diseases in men and others in women. Around that core sit behaviour, the physical environment, socio economic conditions and health services. Genes, age and sex cannot be rewritten, so screening and earlier care work around them while the outer segments remain open to change.

steps.title: Determinants outside the person
steps.tx: **Socio-economic conditions** decide much of health through income, education, occupation and housing. Per capita income, literacy and housing quality track closely with death rates across districts. Health services form another determinant: accessible primary care raises immunisation and early detection. Behaviour and socio-cultural practice, from smoking to food habits, link the social world to the body.
steps.say: Outside forces matter just as much. Income, schooling, occupation and housing track with death rates district by district. Reachable primary care lifts immunisation and early detection. Daily habits, from smoking to food choices, carry social influence into the body.

steps.title: Environment and the right to health
steps.tx: A safe **environment** supplies clean water, clean air and safe food, while a hostile one spreads diarrhoea, respiratory disease and vector borne illness. Health is also a fundamental human right: every person may claim the highest attainable standard of health without distinction of race, religion, political belief or economic condition. That right makes governments, not families alone, responsible for services.
steps.say: Clean water, air and food protect whole communities at once, while polluted surroundings spread diarrhoea and breathing disease. Health also stands as a human right. Each person can claim the highest attainable standard, so governments share responsibility with families.

right.title: Hostile environment
points: Vector borne illness from breeding sites
